extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and methodologists interested in measuring or improving the quality of peer review reports in biomedical research
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply standards for evaluating the quality of peer review reports in biomedical research, and design or select instruments (scales/checklists) to measure that quality. Includes domains of review content, characteristics of reviewers' comments, scoring methods, and tool development/validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer has discussed in the peer review report the importance of the research question and usefulness of the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Did the reviewer give appropriate attention to the importance of the question?' (used to assess whether reviewer commented on study relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer has commented in the peer review report on the originality of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Did the reviewer discuss the originality of the paper?' — used to judge whether reviewer evaluated novelty/added value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of the study results
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer has commented in the peer review report on how authors interpreted and discussed the results of the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The reviewer commented accurately and productively on the quality of the author’s interpretation of the data, including acknowledgment of the data’s limitations.' — assesses correctness and helpfulness of interpretation critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and weaknesses of the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer has identified and commented on the general strong and weak points of the study, with subdomains for methods and statistical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdomains and examples: General — 'How well it identified the study’s strengths and weaknesses?'; Methods — 'Did the reviewer clearly identify strengths and weaknesses in the study’s methods?'; Statistical methods — items inquiring about comments on confidence intervals, p-values, model fit, etc. (noted that statistical-method comments were rare across tools).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and organization of the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer has made comments on data presentation (tables/figures) and manuscript organization/writing communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Are there any constructive suggestions on improvement of a. writing; b. data presentation and c. interpretation' — assesses whether reviewer addresses clarity of presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the reviewer’s comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer has provided organized, structured, and well-formatted comments in the peer review report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Concise well-organized comments to the editor' — evaluates whether comments are logically arranged and usable by authors/editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the reviewer’s comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite domain covering specific qualities of comments: clarity, constructiveness, detail/thoroughness, fairness, knowledgeability, and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdomains and examples: Clarity — 'How clear was this review?'; Constructiveness — 'Were the reviewer’s comments constructive?'; Detail/Thoroughness — 'Detail of commentary'; Fairness — 'Balanced/fair'; Knowledgeability — 'Knowledge of the manuscript’s content area.'; Tone — 'Overall tone of the reviewers was also assessed as harsh or courteous.' These characteristics were among the most frequently included items in existing tools (e.g., detailed/thorough n=11; constructive n=9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of the review report
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer completed the peer review report on time (punctuality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Punctuality of the review' — used both as a standalone domain and as part of some tools' profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of the review report
rubrics_metrics.description: Items inquiring if the reviewer provided a report useful either for editorial decision-making or for improving the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdomains: Decision making — 'The reviewer provided the editor with the proper context and perspective to make a decision about acceptance or revision of the manuscript.'; Manuscript improvement — 'How well the review aids the authors for improving their work and/or writing.' This domain captures whether the report helps editors decide and/or helps authors revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall single-item quality (single-score assessments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-item approach that directly asks an evaluator to score the overall quality of a peer review report (e.g., a 4- or 5-point Likert scale or labels like 'good/fair/poor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review found six tools using a single-item overall score. The authors note this approach provides a subjective overall assessment and many tools using it lacked definition of 'quality' or scoring instructions (example scoring types: 1–4, 1–5, 'good/fair/poor', or 80–100). Considered limited because it lacks component-level detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-item scales vs checklists (tool format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish scales (numeric/nominal overall quality score) from checklists (no overall numeric score); scales typically combine multiple items, checklists present itemized guidance without summarizing to a score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the review 23/24 tools were scales and 1 was a checklist. The authors argue checklists may be more appropriate to avoid problematic summarization/weighting inherent in scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item weighting and overall score calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: How items are weighted and how an overall quality score is derived (sum of scores, mean of scores, single score, or summary score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from included tools: same weight for each item, different weights, or user-defined weights; overall score methods included sum (n=3), mean (n=6), summary score (n=11), single score (n=6). The paper warns that arbitrary weighting/summarization can bias assessments and different weightings produce different quality estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system instructions (defined, partially defined, not defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, operational scoring instructions describing what each score level means (e.g., what constitutes 'Exceptional' vs 'Very good' vs 'Good').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 examples show fully defined descriptors (e.g., 5 Exceptional = 'comprehensive, objective, and insightful... includes comments to the editor'), partially defined examples, and undefined systems. The review found scoring instructions were not defined in 67% of tools; clear instructions improve reproducibility and reduce subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'peer review report quality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit, operational definition of what the tool intends to measure when it labels something 'quality' of a peer review report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of the identified tools reported a clear definition of 'quality'. The article emphasizes that tools should clearly define their target construct (analogous to how RoB defines its aim/domains) to avoid bias and misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool development transparency and method (development process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation of how the tool was developed (e.g., literature review, interviews with editors, iterative rewording, guideline creation, involvement of stakeholders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only one tool reported a rigorous development process (development group, literature review, interviews, revisions and usage guideline). The authors call for transparent, evidence-based development including stakeholder consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation and reliability evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical assessment and reporting of validity (face, content, construct, criterion) and reliability (inter-rater, test–retest, internal consistency) for the assessment tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only 10 tools provided measures of validity/reliability; types included face/content/construct/preliminary criterion validity and inter-rater/test–retest/internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha). The review highlights the lack of criterion validity in all tools and emphasizes the need for demonstrated validity and reliability before tools are used in trials or editorial evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for use as trial outcome or editorial feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the tool is appropriate to be used as an outcome measure in randomized controlled trials of interventions targeting peer review quality, or as a routine editor-facing feedback instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five tools had been used as outcomes in RCTs; the authors caution that use in trials requires validated, reliable, and clearly defined instruments to avoid biased trial results and misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid summarization-weight bias (caution about scoring summaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion that warns against creating or using summary numeric scores that arbitrarily weight heterogeneous items, because different weightings can bias assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note the controversy around scales that summarize items: without empirical justification for weights, summarized scores may produce biased estimates. They recommend considering checklists or carefully justified weighting schemes.
